251.event_title: Tolstoy writes The First Step on giving up meat
251.event: Leo Tolstoy wrote the essay The First Step as the preface to the Russian edition of Howard Williams's book The Ethics of Diet. In it he argued that a good life must begin with self-control, and that the first thing to give up is eating meat, because it requires killing animals against our moral feeling. He closed the essay with a first-person account of his visits to the slaughterhouse at Tula, which he had long put off because he felt ashamed to watch suffering he could not prevent.
251.explanation: One of the world's most admired moral writers argued publicly that a compassionate life and the killing of animals for the table cannot sit together.
251.tie_back: The kural asks how compassion can rule a person who fattens his own flesh on another's, and Tolstoy's essay made the same argument that real kindness has to begin by refusing that flesh.
251._accuracy_note: A strong illustration: Tolstoy argued explicitly that compassion and meat-eating are incompatible, though his frame is self-control rather than the kural's image of rule by compassion.

252.event_title: Benjamin Franklin abandons his vegetarian resolution over fried cod
252.place: Off Block Island, Rhode Island, North America
252.event: As a teenager Benjamin Franklin adopted a vegetable diet after reading the writer Thomas Tryon, and he regarded the killing of fish as a kind of unprovoked murder. On a voyage from Boston, becalmed off Block Island, the crew caught cod, and the smell of the frying fish tempted him. Recalling that smaller fish had been found in the cod's stomachs, he reasoned that if fish ate one another he could eat them, dined heartily, and afterwards returned to a vegetable diet only now and then; in his Autobiography he remarked wryly on how conveniently reason supplies excuses for what one already wants.
252.explanation: Franklin's honest account shows how a principle of kindness to animals can slip away through a single unguarded moment of appetite.
252.tie_back: The kural says that, as unguarded wealth is lost, compassion is not kept by those who eat flesh, and Franklin's resolve gave way exactly when he stopped guarding it.
252._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: it shows a compassionate principle lost through lack of vigilance, though the kural's wealth analogy is only loosely mirrored.

253.event_title: William Hogarth publishes The Four Stages of Cruelty
253.event: William Hogarth published a series of four prints, The Four Stages of Cruelty, following the fictional Tom Nero from a boy who torments animals in the street to an adult who harms people and is finally punished by the law. Hogarth wrote that the prints were meant to reduce the cruel treatment of animals that was common on London's streets, and he had them priced cheaply so that ordinary people could buy them. The series argued that cruelty tolerated in small things, even in children, grows into greater cruelty later.
253.explanation: Hogarth's prints became a classic statement of the idea that harming animals hardens the heart and turns it away from goodness.
253.tie_back: The kural compares the heart of one who relishes another creature's body to that of a man holding a weapon, and Hogarth's series showed the same hardening of the mind toward harm.
253._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the kural's psychological claim that pleasure in harming creatures turns the mind from good, though Hogarth's subject is cruelty to animals rather than eating meat.

254.event_title: Emperor Wu of Liang requires Chinese Buddhist monks to give up all meat
254.event: Emperor Wu of Liang, a devoted Buddhist patron, called assemblies of monks and pressed on them a rule that monastics must abstain from all meat, citing the Nirvana Sutra. Earlier monastic rules had allowed monks to eat so-called clean meat, from animals not killed specifically for them, and some monks objected that the old discipline did not forbid meat. The emperor's rule was enforced and became the lasting norm for Chinese Buddhist monks and nuns.
254.explanation: The decree closed the loophole that eating meat is innocent so long as someone else did the killing, and it shaped Chinese Buddhist practice for the following fifteen centuries.
254.tie_back: The kural says not killing is compassion and adds that eating the flesh of what was killed is also not right, which is exactly the loophole Emperor Wu's rule closed.
254._accuracy_note: A strong fit, since the rule specifically rejected the excuse that meat killed by others may be eaten; sources differ on the exact year (517 or 520).

255.event_title: Emperor Tenmu bans the eating of certain meats in Japan
255.event: In 675 Emperor Tenmu, a devout Buddhist, issued a decree forbidding the eating of cattle, horses, dogs, monkeys and chickens, at first during the farming months of the year. Later rulers strengthened the restriction and it hardened into a broad taboo on meat that lasted in some form for about 1,200 years. The ban was formally ended in 1872 when Emperor Meiji publicly began eating meat.
255.explanation: A single act of restraint, rooted in Buddhist respect for life, spared animals across Japanese society for more than a thousand years.
255.tie_back: One reading of the kural is that the life of creatures is preserved because people refrain from eating flesh, and Japan's long meat taboo is a large-scale example of that preservation.
255._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it fits the commentators' social reading of the first line but says nothing about the kural's warning of inescapable consequence, and deer and boar were not covered by the original decree.

256.event_title: CITES bans the international ivory trade
256.event: After the 1970s and 1980s, when demand for ivory drove the poaching of hundreds of thousands of African elephants, the parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species met in Lausanne in 1989 and moved the African elephant to Appendix I. This effectively banned international commercial trade in ivory, with the listing taking effect in January 1990. In the years that followed, ivory markets shrank and prices fell, and poaching declined in many areas, though later one-off sales and continuing illegal trade weakened the ban's effect.
256.explanation: The ban showed in practice that cutting off the buyers' market is one of the most effective ways to stop the killing.
256.tie_back: The kural argues that no one would kill for money if no one wanted to buy, and the ivory ban put that reasoning into international law.
256._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the kural's demand-and-supply argument, though it concerns ivory rather than meat.

257.event_title: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle exposes the meatpacking industry
257.place: Chicago, Illinois, and Washington, D.C., United States
257.event: Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, first serialised in 1905 and published as a book in 1906, described the conditions inside Chicago's meatpacking plants. Sinclair wrote it to draw attention to the workers, but readers were most shocked by what it revealed about how meat was produced. President Theodore Roosevelt ordered an investigation, and in 1906 Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act.
257.explanation: When the public was made to see clearly where its meat came from, it recoiled and demanded change.
257.tie_back: The kural says people would stop eating flesh if they truly perceived it as another creature's wound, and The Jungle showed how strongly people react when the reality behind meat is laid bare.
257._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the book made people see what lay behind meat, but the response was regulation of hygiene rather than giving up meat.

258.event_title: Plutarch delivers his discourses On the Eating of Flesh
258.event: The Greek writer Plutarch composed two discourses, On the Eating of Flesh, preserved in his Moralia, which argue for abstaining from meat. He asked why people find it strange that Pythagoras refused flesh, argued that the human body is not built like a carnivore's, and condemned the cruelty of killing animals for luxurious meals. The Loeb editors note that these speeches probably date from his youth.
258.explanation: Plutarch's essay is one of the earliest surviving arguments in the West that clear thinking about what meat is should lead a person to refuse it.
258.tie_back: The kural says those whose vision is freed from delusion will not eat flesh separated from life, and Plutarch argued that only habit and blindness keep people eating it.
258._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: it is a written argument rather than a dramatic event, and Plutarch himself later seems to have relaxed his view.

259.event_title: Ashoka's First Rock Edict forbids animal sacrifice
259.place: Mauryan Empire (Girnar and other edict sites), India
259.event: In the first of his Major Rock Edicts, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka proclaimed that in his domain no living beings were to be slaughtered or offered in sacrifice. The same edict recorded that his royal kitchen, where many thousands of animals had once been killed for food, now killed only two peacocks and a deer, and the deer not always, and that in time even these would not be killed.
259.explanation: A great king publicly placed sparing animal life above the sacrificial rites that were then a mark of royal piety.
259.tie_back: The kural ranks not killing one creature above a thousand fire sacrifices, and Ashoka's edict set aside sacrifice itself in favour of not killing.
259._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: the edict directly subordinates sacrifice to the protection of life, though Ashoka has appeared elsewhere in the book for other events.

260.event_title: Francis of Assisi is proclaimed patron of those who promote ecology
260.event: In the apostolic letter Inter Sanctos, Pope John Paul II declared Saint Francis of Assisi the heavenly patron of those who promote ecology. The letter praised Francis for revering nature as a gift of God and pointed to his Canticle of the Creatures. Francis, who died in 1226, had long been remembered for his gentleness toward animals and all living things.
260.explanation: Nearly eight centuries after his death, Francis's reputation for kindness to every creature made him a figure honoured around the world.
260.tie_back: The kural says all living beings will revere the one who harms none, and Francis, remembered for his gentleness to creatures, became a universally honoured symbol of that ideal.
260._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Francis is honoured for gentleness toward creatures, but he is not documented as refusing meat, and the kural's image of animals worshipping is hyperbole no event can match.
